summary: Updates RFC 4090 with extensions that reduce signaling and processing during Fast Reroute facility backup. This improves scalability when many LSPs must switch to backup paths after a link or node failure.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road closes, thousands of cars need new directions. Instead of telling each one, this sends a short summary note.

questions: how to reduce rsvp-te signaling during frr
what is a point of local repair
how does rsvp-te facility backup work
subtitle: Lets MPLS routers reroute thousands of protected tunnels after a failure with one grouped RSVP message instead of one per tunnel.

tldr.problem: After a link or node failure, each protected LSP is signaled individually over the bypass tunnel, which can overwhelm the control plane of the nodes involved when tens of thousands of LSPs are affected.
tldr.mechanism: The Point of Local Repair groups protected LSPs under a Bypass_Group_Identifier, tells the Merge Point in advance using new Extended ASSOCIATION objects, and after a failure activates whole groups with a single B-SFRR-Active object and summary refresh.
tldr.outcome: Signaling between the two nodes becomes independent of the number of protected LSPs. It updates RFC 4090 and stays backward compatible with nodes that do not support it.

today: RFC 8796 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4090, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem After a Failure
sections.content:
The Fast Reroute (FRR) procedures of RFC 4090 let a Point of Local Repair (PLR) move traffic and signaling of a protected RSVP-TE Label Switched Path (LSP) onto a bypass tunnel after a link or node failure. That signaling is done separately for each protected LSP, which can cause scalability and latency problems on the PLR and on the Merge Point (MP) where the bypass tunnel rejoins the path.

The RFC describes a large deployment where one router may host tens of thousands of protected LSPs leaving through the same link, while also acting as an MP for a similar number arriving on that link. After a failure the control plane is busy rerouting and merging, head-end routers then try to reconverge the LSPs, and other protocols such as the IGP converge at the same time.

The fix is to let the PLR assign protected LSPs to a bypass tunnel group, tell the MP about it, and then signal per group instead of per LSP. It builds on the summary refresh of RFC 2961, which uses MESSAGE_ID values to refresh state cheaply.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bridge closes and a traffic officer has to wave every car individually, he gets overwhelmed. This RFC lets him wave a whole group at once.

sections.title: Groups and Extended ASSOCIATION Objects
sections.content:
The extension carries its data in the Extended ASSOCIATION object (from RFC 4872 and RFC 6780). Two new Association Types are defined: B-SFRR-Ready (value 5) and B-SFRR-Active (value 6).

The PLR creates and manages the groups, each identified by a Bypass_Group_Identifier. A PLR SHOULD give the same identifier to all protected LSPs that share the same outgoing protected interface, are protected by the same bypass tunnel, and use the same tunnel sender address for backup path identification. This keeps the number of groups, and so the signaling, small.

Before a failure the PLR puts a B-SFRR-Ready object in the Path message of each protected LSP, and the MP acknowledges it in the Resv message. After a failure the PLR sends a B-SFRR-Active object in the Path message of the bypass tunnel itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The PLR puts cars with the same route into numbered groups ahead of time and tells the other end which car is in which group.

sections.title: The Two Association IDs
sections.content:
The IPv4 B-SFRR-Ready Extended Association ID holds a 16-bit Bypass_Tunnel_ID, 16 reserved bits (zero on send, ignored on receipt), the bypass tunnel source and destination addresses, a 32-bit Bypass_Group_Identifier, and a MESSAGE_ID object from RFC 2961. The IPv6 form is the same with 128-bit addresses.

The B-SFRR-Active ID starts with a 16-bit Num-BGIDs count and 16 reserved bits, then that many 32-bit Bypass_Group_Identifier values. After them come a replacement RSVP_HOP object, a replacement TIME_VALUES object and the tunnel sender address (IPv4 or IPv6). The replacement objects apply to every LSP in the listed groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The first note says 'car 12 is in group 7, using detour X'. The second note says 'groups 7 and 8, go now, and here is the new return address'.

sections.title: Handshake Before Failure
sections.content:
Summary FRR can only be used after a handshake between PLR and MP. The PLR adds B-SFRR-Ready to the protected LSP's Path message, with a MESSAGE_ID whose Flags are cleared. It MUST generate a new Message_Identifier whenever the contents change, for example when the bypass assignment changes.

The MP checks that the bypass tunnel exists and that the group is not already FRR Active, builds a mirrored group database per PLR, records the MESSAGE_ID, and answers with B-SFRR-Ready in the Resv message. All fields except the MESSAGE_ID are copied from the Path message. The PLR treats the LSP as Summary FRR capable only if everything but the MESSAGE_ID matches, and otherwise, or if the object is absent from a later refresh, it MUST treat the LSP as not capable.

The PLR MUST ensure the bypass assignment can satisfy the protected LSP's MTU requirements after rerouting. Each node SHOULD strip B-SFRR-Ready objects that name its own addresses when forwarding, so they do not travel further.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any road closes, the two ends agree on the group list and both confirm they have the same list.

sections.title: Rerouting After Failure
sections.content:
On detecting a fault the PLR first applies the object modification of RFC 4090 Section 6.4.3, using a common RSVP_HOP and SENDER_TEMPLATE for Summary FRR LSPs on the same bypass tunnel. It MUST signal non-Summary FRR LSPs over the bypass tunnel before the Summary FRR ones, in case a recent assignment change has not yet been processed.

Instead of one Path message per LSP, the PLR adds B-SFRR-Active objects to the bypass tunnel's own Path message. Several such objects can share one message. The PLR then starts sending Srefresh messages with the stored Message_Identifiers.

On receiving it, the MP performs normal merge processing for each LSP in each group as if it had received individual Path messages. It copies the RSVP_HOP, the TIME_VALUES and the tunnel sender address, modifies the ERO as in RFC 4090, and activates the stored MESSAGE_IDs. A failure when merging any LSP MUST produce a PathErr. No individual Resv messages are sent, and the MP SHOULD immediately use summary refresh for the Resv state.

If the MP's refresh dropped the Ready object just as a fault hit, the MP answers the unknown Message_Identifier with an Srefresh NACK, and the PLR replays the full Path state.
sections.plainLanguage: When the road closes, the officer shouts 'groups 7 and 8, detour now!' once, and everyone in those groups follows.

sections.title: Compatibility, Security and IANA
sections.content:
The ASSOCIATION object class number has the form 11bbbbbb, so nodes that do not support it ignore it and forward it unchanged, as unknown-class rules in RFC 2205 require. That makes the extension backward compatible.

Intercepting a message reveals slightly more about network state. Because a group can be rerouted with a single message, an intruder could affect a whole group at once, although the RFC notes this is already possible with per-LSP signaling at greater cost. Existing RSVP integrity and authenticity mechanisms (RFC 2747) can be applied, and RFC 4090 and RFC 5920 considerations also apply.

IANA added the two Association Types to the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry: 5 for B-SFRR-Ready and 6 for B-SFRR-Active.
sections.plainLanguage: Older routers that do not understand the new notes simply pass them along, so nothing breaks.

items.desc: Bypass Summary FRR Ready: records the group assignment.

items.label: B-SFRR-Active
items.desc: Bypass Summary FRR Active: reroutes groups over the bypass tunnel.
